# Age-related macular degeneration

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ophthalmology > Retina and vision > Age-related macular degeneration*

[Original Article Link](/library/GO0BFT)

---

## Summary

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disease of the <u>retina</u> and represents the most common cause of blindness in individuals > 65 years in developed countries. It is classified into two major forms: dry AMD and wet AMD. Dry AMD is caused by deposition of various metabolites under the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u> (<u>drusen</u>) and usually develops over decades, while wet AMD is caused by neovascularizations growing into the subretinal space and manifests within weeks to months or even acutely. Both forms ultimately cause impaired central <u>vision</u> and can, in rare cases, lead to complete blindness. <u>Patient history</u> and clinical tools such as the <u>Amsler grid</u> can provide clues regarding visual impairment. <u>Fundoscopy</u> is needed to identify specific pathological changes. <u>Fluorescein angiography</u> may be used to confirm the diagnosis of wet AMD. Treatment focuses on slowing <u>vision loss</u> and/or improving <u>vision</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

AMD is the leading cause of blindness in individuals > 65 years in developed countries.




* Age of onset: : usually > 55 years [[1]](/library/exXxvZ0)

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 1.47% [[2]](/library/UxXbDZ0)

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> [[1]](/library/exXxvZ0)





Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Multifactorial

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Advanced age

* <u>Family history</u> and genetic predisposition

* Cardiovascular disease

* Smoking

* <u>Obesity</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

AMD is characterized by progressive degenerative changes in the central part of the <u>retina</u> (<u>macula</u>) → visual impairment.




* Dry AMD (∼ 90%)

* Also referred to as nonexudative AMD or <u>atrophic</u> AMD

* Deposition of yellow-whitish material consisting of lipids, vitronectin, and other <u>proteins</u> (drusen) in the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u> and between it and <u>Bruch membrane</u>;   → slow progressive <u>atrophy</u> of the local <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u> (centrally or pericentrally)

* Wet AMD (∼ 10%)

* Also referred to as <u>exudative</u> AMD or neovascular AMD

* Choroidal <u>neovascularization</u> (between the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u> and <u>Bruch's membrane</u>) → leaking of <u>intravascular</u> serous fluid and blood;   → sudden localized elevation of the <u>macula</u> and/or detachment of the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u>

## Clinical features

* Painless central or pericentral visual impairment  ; → reduced <u>visual acuity</u>, difficulty adapting to changes in lighting 

* Dry AMD: slow progressive visual impairment (usually over decades) and unilateral or bilateral onset

* Wet AMD: acute ;   or insidious onset (over weeks to months) and usually manifests in one <u>eye</u> first

* Metamorphopsia: type of visual distortion in which straight lines appear wavy, which can be tested for using an <u>Amsler grid</u>

* <u>Scotoma</u> (<u>blind spot</u>)





References:[[3]](/library/YsantN)

---

## Diagnosis

### Both, wet and dry AMD




* Amsler grid: detection of <u>metamorphopsias</u> and <u>scotomas</u>

* <u>Fundoscopy</u>

* Dry AMD

* <u>Drusen</u>

* <u>Retinal pigment epithelium</u> <u>atrophy</u>

* <u>Retinal pigment epithelium</u> <u>hypertrophy</u> (mottling)

* Wet AMD

* Grayish-green retinal discoloration

* Serous detachment of the <u>retina</u> and the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u>

* Subretinal and <u>intraretinal hemorrhage</u> and/or <u>exudate</u>

* Fibrous disciform scars





### If wet AMD is suspected




* Fluorescence <u>angiography</u>  

* Dry AMD: well-defined hyperfluorescence of the altered <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u>

* Wet AMD: <u>neovascularization</u> and exudation (diffuse hyperfluorescence) in the macular region

* Color fundus photography: enables evaluation of disease progression and interpretation of <u>fluorescein angiography</u>

* <u>Optical coherence tomography</u> (<u>OCT</u>) 

* Detection of intraretinal or subretinal fluid retention

* Helps confirm diagnosis of wet AMD  and to monitor progress under treatment

## Differential diagnoses

| Differential diagnosis of vision loss |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condition | Clinical features | <u>Fundoscopy</u> |
| AMD | <br><br>* May be insidious (dry AMD) or rapid (wet AMD) onset<br><br>* Impairment of central <u>vision</u> only (<u>vision loss</u> is rare)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Drusen</u><br><br>* <u>Macula</u> depigmentation<br><br><br> |
| <u>Open-angle glaucoma</u> | <br><br>* Insidious onset<br><br>* Peripheral <u>vision loss</u> (tunnel <u>vision</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* Disc cupping with high <u>intraocular pressure</u><br><br> |
| <u>Central retinal artery occlusion</u> | <br><br>* Acute or subacute onset<br><br>* Complete <u>vision loss</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Swollen disc<br><br>* <u>Retinal hemorrhages</u><br><br>* <u>Cotton wool spots</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Retinal detachment</u> | <br><br>* Acute onset<br><br>* Partial or complete <u>vision loss</u> (falling curtain)<br><br><br> | <br>* Detached or floating <u>retina</u><br><br> |
| <u>Cataract</u> | <br><br>* Insidious onset<br><br>* Blurred, dim <u>vision</u>, and a glare<br><br>* Absent or opacified <u>red-reflex</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Retina</u> may not be visible (in advanced disease)<br><br> |




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

No causal treatment is available.




* Supportive treatment

* Patient education

* Visual and reading aids: magnifying glass

* Avoid <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., smoking)

* Improve diet (i.e., high in green leafy vegetables and fish)

* Antioxidants therapy: <u>vitamins</u> A, C, and E, <u>beta-carotene</u>, <u>zinc</u>

* Treatment of wet AMD

* First-line: injection of <u>VEGF</u> inhibitors (ranibizumab, <u>bevacizumab</u>, pegaptanib) into the <u>vitreous body</u>

* Second-line: when <u>VEGF</u> is contraindicated

* Laser coagulation: direct thermal coagulation of <u>neovascularization</u>

* Photodynamic therapy: intravenously administered dye is activated in the <u>eye</u> by laser light → local toxic effect → <u>thrombosis</u> of subretinal neovascularizations
